utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, sir, concerns when these foreigners became a problem. And I'm trying to get from you an answer to the question at what point the foreigners became a significant problem for the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreigners became a significant problem for the 3rd Corps when we discovered that HVO officers had been kidnapped. By those foreigners, naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to that point in time, sir, were you personally involved in any investigations or any efforts to find out about potential crimes involving these foreigners prior to the HVO kidnappings in the middle of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, apart from the requests to release people from HVO prisons, I can't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to ask you about some events in February 1993 in Bijelo Bucje, does that refresh your recollection in any way?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that it was in that month. I remember a different problem in the Bijelo Bucje area, towards the end of August, if I'm not mistaken, when an operations officer from the 3rd Corps who was visiting the units discovered that there were problems there. But at the time, the El Mujahid detachment had already been formed. That was at the end of August, if I remember correctly. Or perhaps it was the beginning of September. I can't remember the exact date, but I do know there were problems at the time with that group of foreigners. But at that time, the El Mujahid detachment had already been formed. As for other details, I can't remember. I can't remember any other events, but I wouldn't exclude that possibility. However, I didn't receive any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall being involved in any kind of investigation or inquiries concerning the murder of two British citizens in the area of Travnik in February of 1993 in which the conclusion was that the crimes were committed by foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had received information according to which two Englishmen had been killed. As I said, the services continued to investigate matters. I don't know what information these services obtained. I don't know whether they discovered that the group of foreigners we had been referring to committed this act or someone else. But I did have the opportunity of seeing those two Englishmen who were killed. They were transferred to the Zenica hospital, and that was the first time that I saw them, in the Zenica hospital. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, sir: You told us earlier that you and the leadership of the corps were unaware of the location of these foreigners, and also the precise number of these foreigners. And you told us about that on the 9th of December. Do you remember telling the Trial Chamber that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said, sir, that the foreigners were highly mobile.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you told us that you were unaware of their location and their numbers, did that remain the case through 1993 or was that limited to a certain point in time? In other words, did there come a time when you knew where they were located and you knew how many of them or approximately how many of them there were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as 1992 and 1993 is concerned, well, I didn't know their exact location at that time. I knew they were somewhere in the Travnik Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond area. But I don't know whether it was at the end of 1993 or at the beginning of 1994 when their main location was in Zenica, in the Podbrezje area. I have testified about this before the Court. I couldn't give you an exact date, but it was either towards the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994. That was the first time I had the opportunity of visiting that unit in Podbrezje, at the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, sir, when you say visiting "that unit," are you referring to the El Mujahid detachment, or the El Mujahid unit?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the unit I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the end of 1993/1994, you're telling us you did not know where these foreigners were within the 3rd Corps' zone of responsibility. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I personally did not know where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said, sir, that you weren't aware or you didn't know how many of them there were, can you give us a rough idea or a rough approximation as to the information the 3rd Corps had about the number of these foreigners that were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the ABiH 3rd Corps ever had any information on the number of foreigners in the El Mujahid detachment in 1993 or 1994 or 1995. I don't think anyone knew how many foreigners there were in the El Mujahid detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're telling me that there was a unit of the 3rd Corps, and the leadership of the 3rd Corps didn't know how many people were in that unit?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my duty within the 3rd Corps to know how many men there were in all the units. And the El Mujahid detachment, as part of the 3rd Corps, was composed of those foreigners and of the local population. I don't know how many foreigners there were in that 3rd Corps unit, in that El Mujahid unit. All I can say is that I don't remember that the 3rd Corps ever had detailed information on the number of foreigners who were in that 3rd Corps unit, in the 3rd Corps unit that was called the El Mujahid unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, sir, about prior to the formation of that unit, in the first, say, six or seven months of 1993. How many foreigners were in Central Bosnia? And again, I'm talking about armed foreigners, not humanitarian workers. How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. And I think that we have defined this group of foreigners. As I said, according to the information we had, and in particular the information obtained by the 3rd Corps Operations Group, as far as I know, it wasn't possible for them to assess the number of foreigners present in the 3rd Corps' zone of responsibility. I said that in mid-June 1993, I personally saw them by the church in Guca Gora. I said that I saw between 10 and 15 of them but I don't know what kind of information the security service within the 3rd Corps had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can, sir, if you can give us a rough approximation, that would be helpful. Were there 20 of them? Were there 200? Were there 2.000? Were there 20.000? Were there more than 200.000? How many of these people were there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, I could make a rough estimate. We didn't even have 200.000 men in the ABiH -- or in the 3rd Corps -- I mean, in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. It's very difficult for me to provide you with an exact number. There weren't 200.000 of them. There weren't 20.000 of them. There weren't 5.000 of them. Perhaps there were between 50 and a hundred of them. Now you'll ask me how I know this. I'm telling you that I don't have any such information. I can't give you a precise estimate. I can tell you that there weren't 200.000 of them, but there weren't 5.000 of them either. But as to how many of them there were, I couldn't say. I saw a group consisting of 10 to 15 of them. And on that basis, I could conclude that there were 10 to 15 or more. Perhaps there were 50 or a hundred of them. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, perhaps the very fact that when they were put into the unit, the El Mujahid detachment, can give us some occasion as to the number of them. They weren't formed into a brigade-sized unit or a battalion-sized unit; they were formed into something smaller than a battalion. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in military terminology, a detachment is a smaller unit than a battalion. Therefore, those are units the size of about two companies. In other words, 220 to 250 people. But I said that in those detachments -- in that detachment, El Mujahid, there were not only foreigners, there were also Bosniaks, locals, who joined the unit. So we're talking about a number of approximately 250 men in the El Mujahid unit. Not all of them were foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. Your estimate was of the roughly 250 men that were in the El Mujahid detachment, 50 to 100 of them were foreigners. I don't want to put words in your mouth, sir, but that's what you've told us; there were perhaps 50 or 100 of them. If you want to correct that, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I said. I said only what I've seen. And I gave only a rough assessment of how many men there could have been in the El Mujahid unit, and the only thing I actually claimed was that not all of them were foreigners. The majority of them were locals from Bosnia and Herzegovina. If there were 250 or so in total, I can't say that 50 to 100 were foreigners and all the others were Bosniaks or people from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm just saying that I have no information that the 3rd Corps ever knew exactly the number of foreigners within the El Mujahid unit. Maybe some other service within the 3rd Corps knew that. Maybe some other service who was directly assigned that job, whose job it was to know. But I can't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you've told us that the number of foreigners in Central Bosnia was between 50 and 100, approximately. That's all I'm asking. I don't necessarily need a specific number, because you've told us you can't give a specific number. Just an approximate number, and you've told us on two occasions, on page 48, that there were between 50 and 100 foreigners.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really find these questions very difficult. But let us conclude this discussion. I cannot confirm anything. I just explained to you my thinking. I know that there were no such armed foreigners - I already explained what I mean by that - in the area of the 3rd Corps. But obviously, there was a problem for the 3rd Corps. Maybe other corps encountered similar problems. I only told you as much as I knew. I assume, as I said, there were 50 to 100, so we can leave it at that. These questions are really very difficult for me. You're asking me to say something that I cannot say with any certainty. I'm just giving you my opinion. I told you what I know and what I have seen. I have already said before this Honourable Court what I know and what I have seen. And when I cannot remember something, I'll indicate that. And if you want to quote me as saying that there were 50 to 100, then let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the mobility of these foreigners, and I'm talking now, sir, about the time period prior to the formation of the El Mujahid detachment; that is, the first, say, six or seven months of 1993. You told us that the foreigners were mobile within the area of Central Bosnia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that those were figures. That was the information that was available to me; that they were mobile and they were moving around Central Bosnia. However, I had no occasion to see it with my own eyes. What I can state with certainty is that I had some reports to that effect. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those reports provide you with any information as to how these people moved about in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not exactly reports. As a soldier, I have a totally different understanding of the word "report." When I receive a report, there is some information indicated in it, as opposed to some intelligence I received in some other way through some other channels. However, our intelligence service at that point was not able to give us exact numbers of these people or their location, so the service who was in charge of making assessments or evaluations tried to give us an estimate of their Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond mobility and number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, my question is: How did they move about? How did they get from one place to another? Did the information that you had provide any insight into how these people moved around?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have information of that degree of detail. Nothing that would tell me how they moved through Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea, sir, how they got through the various HVO checkpoints that you've talked about that were in Central Bosnia? Do you have any idea how, or did you have any information as to how they were able to get through HVO checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified before this Honourable Court how these foreigners were able to come into Bosnia and Herzegovina in the first place. I said they were stopped and checked at every checkpoint held by the Croatian Defence Council. I can only say that they must have been arrested, too, taken to military prisons, because later on, exchanges took place in the area of the 3rd Corps involving foreigners and observers from the European Union Monitoring Mission, which only goes to show that the HVO had good information about those foreigners, and it is certain that they must have entered Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, I suppose that the HVO was much better informed than we were in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you just a couple of questions about that. You've told us that these people, these foreigners, must have come into the country from Croatia, and it was also the case, was it not, that when the war in Bosnia first started in 1992, in the spring of 1992, the Bosniaks and the Croats for the most part were allied against the Serbian forces in Bosnia? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian -- rather, HVO units and the units of the ABiH had not joined yet at that time, and they did not perform joint operations, as far as I know, at least not in the area of responsibility which I controlled, first as commander of the staff, and later as deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. There had been attempts to unite the two forces, but they had not been successful at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, were the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims united, as a general rule, in defending themselves against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not united. But they were defending themselves from the aggressor. That's true. But at that time, they were not united.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims were not cooperating to defend themselves against the Bosnian Serbs in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it was a slip of tongue -- slip of the tongue on my part. I meant the HVO and the units of the Territorial Defence of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In TO units, there were Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. All patriotically oriented citizens of Bosnia from all three ethnic communities were represented in units of the TO. That was the reality at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to object because the witness said HVO and the Army of the BH were not united but they were fighting a common aggressor. The question that followed from my colleague, whether they were united, did not follow from the witness's answer. Since he asked whether they were united, he was not relying on the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have an objection from the Defence. Mr. Mundis, what do you have to say in response to the objection at page 52:24, line 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I don't really have much to add, Mr. President. There's no necessary requirement that one question follow from another question. The witness's answer was such that he basically said there had been attempts to unite the forces, they had been unsuccessful, and my question was, as a general rule, were the peoples united? It's a different question. It's not one that was designed to confuse the witness. I believe the witness has gone on and clarified the answer so that, in the event there was any confusion, it seems to have disappeared in light of the witness's clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, the witness did clarify his answer from line 18, page 52. It is now 5.30. We're going to take the break now because we have been sitting for an hour and a half almost. And we'll resume at 5 to 6.00 or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can resume our hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I suggest to you that the mujahedin -- or excuse me, the foreigners came into Bosnia as early as the summer of 1992 to join in the fight against the Serbs in Bosnia. Would you agree with that comment?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know that. But I said that after an awful catastrophe that happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, many people in the world wanted to help actively Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would include these foreign fighters, these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all came to help Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us over several days that these foreigners from April -- mid-April onwards, 1993 -- mid-April 1993 onwards, caused problems for the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Serious problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told us last Thursday, and let me actually read from the transcript of what you said. This is the testimony of the 9th of December, page 60, lines 11 through 14. You said: "The 3rd Corps did not have enough capabilities to deal with the problem, and we said that to our superior command at the first meeting that we had with the topic of foreigners on the agenda." And my question, sir, is what did you mean when you said "The 3rd Corps did not have enough capabilities to deal with the problem..."?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Capabilities," though, is a broad term. We did not have enough forces, we did not have enough information; how many men there were, how well-trained they are, how well-equipped. We got all our information from the competent service, one of whose assignments was to find out who these people were who were causing us problems, and that is something that I already talked about. The 3rd Corps at the time did not have enough resources, and therefore did not have the capability to deal with the problem. That's the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, I assume, and I'm sure you'll correct me if I'm wrong, but I assume that the HVO and the Bosnian Croat civilian population also viewed these foreigners as a problem.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I share that opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would seem as though the problems associated with these foreigners was a mutual problem of the ABiH and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say yes or no to this question. It is a complex problem. I said we didn't know how many of those people had entered and in which way. I said the HVO was controlling entry to the Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were better placed to assess how many of them were entering and what kind of men they were. Much better placed than we were in the 3rd Corps. They probably were a problem to the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, just as they were for us, the Bosniak people. To whom they represented a greater problem, it is now difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, certainly in light of the conclusions that the 3rd Corps reached, that these people were responsible for crimes committed against Bosnian Croat civilians or surrendered HVO soldiers, they would certainly be a problem for the Bosnian Croat population and the HVO as a whole.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's true. In addition to the fact that the HVO controlled their entry into Bosnia and Herzegovina, if we speak about Miletici village, they were closer to the HVO in that locality. And they could as easily investigate those crimes as we had tried to investigate them in the 3rd Corps. I have no knowledge, though, whether the HVO Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond really investigated those crimes or not. I simply have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us on Friday that it was possible when the ABiH and the HVO identified issues of mutual concern, to try to work together to solve these problems.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the ability to cooperate, but in fact, we did not receive complete information from the HVO as to how many foreigners had entered. I mean, the same kind of foreigners that you mean, how many of them had entered Bosnia and Herzegovina. So in that area, we did not cooperate, although I agree we could have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That brings me to my next point, sir: Would it have been possible, or did you ever -- let me ask it that way: Did you ever propose to Colonel Blaskic or Colonel Nakic a cease-fire so that the 3rd Corps could solve the problem presented by these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I can't remember if there was such a possibility. I can't remember that we discussed the problem of the foreigners in that way, in those terms. I know that they represented a problem to both sides. How they dealt with it, I don't know. I know how we tried to deal with it. Obviously, we did not cooperate enough in that area. At the time when they were entering, we were not able to check who they were, how many, what kind of documents they had. At the state border of Croatia, the Croatians were at least able to see their passports, to see their names. We didn't even have the ability to do that. We didn't even know on what kind of passports they entered, what names were in those passports. When I told earlier that they were told at some point that they should show their documents and if they weren't willing to do so, they should leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, I know that one group who was unwilling to comply were eventually expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, my question was: Did you ever propose a cease-fire to Colonel Blaskic or Colonel Nakic so that the 3rd Corps could solve the problems presented by the foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. But I don't rule out that possibility. I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall ever proposing to Colonel Blaskic or Colonel Nakic that the ABiH 3rd Corps and the HVO Central Bosnia operational zone units undertake joint operations to concentrate their forces on resolving once and for all the problem presented by these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask these questions, sir, because you've told us that the 3rd Corps did not have the capabilities to solve this problem; you've told us that there were 50 to 100 of these foreigners. And it would seem that if the 20-plus thousand soldiers of the 3rd Corps couldn't solve it by themselves that a combined force of the HVO and the ABiH in Central Bosnia might be able to do the job.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony that was just quoted here refers to 1994, early 1994. I said that in 1993, before the establishment of the El Mujahid detachment, we were not aware of what kind of troops they were. We were trying to find out the details, and I testified before this Court that we had had information that they were handing out money to the people, food, that they were marrying young girls from local families, especially families that had many children or large families, and we didn't know exactly to what extent they were intermarrying, but we knew that that was going on. We did not have enough forces to confront them. We needed a lot of resources, equipment, and troops to face the aggressor. And we were not in a position to open up a third front line. Can you imagine a soldier who is, of his own free will, opening up a third front line if he's not able to handle the two existing ones facing one of the best-trained and one of the best-equipped armies of the world? As I said, we did not have enough real information to confront this group of armed foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back then and ask you once again, in the first six months of 1993, how many foreigners - and again, armed foreigners - were in Central Bosnia? Because now you seem to be saying that the number 50 to a hundred was in response to early 1994. I want to be very clear: I'm talking about the first six months of 1993. What is your best estimate of the number of armed foreigners in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've put a precise question to me. We were talking about the El Mujahid detachment. I must remind you that this detachment was formed at the beginning of August 1993. In the first half of 1993, we had no information. It was very difficult to assess how many foreigners there were. I don't know how many foreigners there were at the beginning or in the middle of 1993. I said that while I was in the 3rd Corps, I, at least, had no information according to which we knew the exact number of foreigners who were in the El Mujahid unit. And it's even more difficult for me to know how many of them there were before the formation of the El Mujahid detachment. You're asking me to tell you about something that I know nothing about. I can't tell you about something that I have no knowledge about. I can tell you about things that I know. I can provide you with the information I have. I don't know how many foreigners there were in mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. General, on page 47, beginning at line 9, I asked you a series of questions concerning these numbers. And the first one of those questions was, "Prior to the formation of that unit, in the first six or seven months of 1993, how many foreigners were in Central Bosnia?" You then told us that you only were aware of the 10 to 15 you saw in Guca Gora. I asked you to give us a rough approximation. That's line 21 of page 47. I then threw out some hypothetical numbers. You might remember that. You responded, beginning on line 25 of page 47 and continued until page 48. And you told us on lines 10 and 11 -- excuse me, 9, 10, and 11, that there were perhaps 50 or a hundred of them. You also told us on page 48 at line 5, there were 50 or a hundred of them. Those were all in response to a question that indicated I was talking about the first six months of 1993. Are you now telling us that you don't know how many foreigners were in Central Bosnia in the first six months of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect for my learned colleague, I think that this is at least the 20th time that the same question has been put to the witness. The witness has answered each of these questions and said what he knew and what he didn't know. In order to say something in response to all these questions, he provided a number. But it's quite clear from all his answers that he cannot provide an exact number. I don't understand why the Prosecution keeps putting the same questions to this witness given that the answers the witness provides are always the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, are you going to pursue this matter? The witness has said that he believed there were between 50 and a hundred of them, but nothing very precise has been stated. In fact, you have put this question to the witness at least ten times, but on each occasion, the witness answered the question in imprecise terms. General, in order to clarify this issue, the answer everyone would like to have is, as far as you know, how many mujahedin were there at the beginning of 1993, in the first six months of 1993? If I say "mujahedin," let's say a group of foreigners, since that's what you said. As far as you can remember, what sort of approximate number could you give us? And then we'll move on to something else. In the first half of 1993, as far as you know, how many foreigners were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am telling you with full responsibility that I don't know how many groups there were or how many people were in the groups. All I can say is that in mid-June in 1993, I saw a group of between 10 and 15 men. This was in front of the church in Guca Gora. And I don't really know how many of them there were after that event. It's difficult for me to make an assessment. If I made a mistake, I apologise. I was talking about the period when the El Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Mujahid detachment was formed. And I again said that there were between 50 and a hundred of them. But similarly, I said that no one ever knew the exact number of foreigners present in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. At least, I wasn't aware of any such information. I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This notion, sir, of opening a third front against these foreigners, was this a topic that was discussed among the 3rd Corps leadership in early 1993 or middle of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we didn't discuss this at the beginning of 1993. We discussed this matter when we realised that this was a real problem. This was in mid-1993. And at the time, we had information according to which they had contact with our local population. I have already said that they would distribute food, money, they would marry young girls. We didn't know how many young girls they'd married, we didn't know how much money they had distributed or how much food they had distributed. But you must understand that at the time the population had nothing to eat. I also said that the 3rd Corps wasn't in a position to provide the people with food and money. They didn't have enough food for their own soldiers, let alone for the people. So we knew that if we tried to confront such a group of armed men at the time, we didn't know how many of the local inhabitants would join them. We didn't want a war between members of the 3rd Corps and the people who supported those foreigners. We believed that we had to find a different solution to that problem. It wasn't possible to open a third front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn now to the monastery at Guca Gora. Do you remember in June 1993 a BritBat officer by the name of Major Vaughan Kent-Payne?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met a lot of English officers. I may have met him. I may have seen him. Perhaps I did meet him. Perhaps I did see him. I don't know who this officer is. If I saw him, perhaps I'd be able to remember whether I had seen him or not. I know that there were a lot of officers that I had contact with. We either spoke to each other personally or they were members of a mission or a member of some international commission. I really met a lot of English officers. And perhaps I also met this officer among that large group of English officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Major Kent-Payne testified before this Tribunal that he had a discussion with you about the damage done to the monastery in Guca Gora. And according to Major Kent-Payne - and this is page 4818 of the transcripts - you told Major Kent-Payne that it was not regular troops that caused the damage, but it was the foreigners, the mujahedin, according to the transcript. Do you remember -- this was in the 3rd Corps headquarters building that he relates this discussion. Does that refresh your recollection in any way of the discussion that you may have had with Major Kent-Payne?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you provide me with a date? Tell me when I spoke to Mr. Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe it was in mid-June. Let me see if I can find that. His testimony was at the end of June 1993, about the 30th of June. And that's page 4817.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. At the time, I certainly told Major Kent-Payne that the ABiH was not inflicting damage on religious buildings. I said that, as far as I knew, the ABiH was taking measures to protect religious buildings. This was what we ordered ABiH troops to do. I can't remember the substance of my discussion with Mr. Kent-Payne, but I said that ABiH units were not involved in this destruction. They would not destroy religious buildings because when we found out that ABiH members engaged in such activities, we would take the necessary measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me read to you from the transcript of what Major Kent-Payne testified that you said to him when he was at the 3rd Corps headquarters at the end of June, perhaps the 30th of June, 1993. This is a quote from his testimony. Major Kent-Payne said: "And I said to him" - meaning you - "words to the effect of `but they're under your control, and therefore you are responsible for doing this'. And he said an analogy on the lines of `but you have to understand that, that the foreigners are like the genie in Aladdin, then. You can rub the lamp and get the genie out to help you. But unlike the genie who returns to the lamp then, the foreigners are very difficult to get back into their box, and they're difficult to control'. And he said that `it was something that they needed to -- to work on, to ensure that these people did not behave in a manner which -- which was -- which was unbecoming and which was against the Geneva Convention'." Now, sir -- for the benefit of the record, this is page 4818, lines 13 through 23. General, let me ask you if you recall a conversation with Major Kent-Payne that went along the lines of what Major Kent-Payne has testified about.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exclude the possibility of having said something to that effect when speaking to Mr. -- or rather, Major Kent-Payne. I don't remember the details of that conversation. It took place a long time ago. I'm not familiar with the symbolism of Aladdin's lamp. I'm not sure that that is what I said, or maybe he said that that's the impression I gave when I spoke to him. I can't remember what I said exactly, if I did mention Aladdin and his lamp. I can't remember what the symbolism would have been. Perhaps I wanted to say that the issue of the foreigners was a complex issue, if they were there, and we had information according to which they were present in June 1993. We wanted to control and prevent them from violating international rules and international humanitarian law. That's probably what I discussed with him. I can't remember the exact words that were used when I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me now take you to the day that you went to Guca Gora and saw the mujahedin for the first time. And you testified on Thursday, page 43, that it was a few days after the 9th of June 1993. This is the day you saw the mujahedin -- or the foreigners at the monastery. Is that an accurate reflection of your testimony? It was a few days after the 9th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had seen them during that period of time, but I don't remember saying that I saw them in the monastery. I remember saying that I saw them in front of the monastery. If I said that I had seen them in the monastery a few days ago, then that was a slip of the tongue. That was a mistake. I saw them in front of the monastery. This is an important difference. I don't understand English, so I don't know whether I said "in the monastery" or "in front of the monastery." Your Honours, if I said "in the monastery," that was an error. I did not see them in the monastery, I saw them in front of the monastery. Perhaps I made a mistake, but this is an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me correct myself. The testimony in English says, on page 44, line 4, "At the entrance from the eastern side in the yard of the church." Now, let me ask you this, sir: Is that the courtyard of the monastery, the enclosed courtyard of the monastery, or is that at the front door in front of the monastery?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me be quite clear and quite precise: The first time I mentioned this, I was very precise. I mentioned the main entrance to the monastery, which is to the south. You enter the entrance from the road, there's some steps, and that's the entrance to the church. There's an entrance to the east. I can make you a sketch. I remember this very well because that is the first time I met that group of foreigners, and everyone had been speaking about those foreigners for about six months. They had been mentioning foreigners, mujahedin, et cetera. I hadn't seen them. That's why I mentioned this event. I said that the gate from the eastern side, that's where I saw them. I'd entered the courtyard -- I'd entered the courtyard of the church, but I didn't enter the church. They were in the courtyard from the eastern side. That's what I think I said, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond because I still have this image in my mind. We all have immense problems, and I can't forget the first image I had when I saw that group of foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you be a little more specific in terms of the date that you were actually in the courtyard at the Guca Gora monastery? You told us on the 9th of December, page 43, that it was "a few days after 9 June, 1993." Can you be any more specific?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I said that on the 9th of June 1993, I was there when the civilians were evacuated. I can't remember whether that was two or three days after that date, but in any event, it was after that date. It was after the 9th of June 1993. In my notes, for example, it might say that I was there on the 9th, but I can't remember the exact date. I've already said that I didn't know the date. But it was two or three days after that date, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- so I take it, then, sir, it would be somewhere around the 11th or 12th of June 1993 when you saw these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time you arrived at the courtyard of the Guca Gora monastery on the 11th or 12th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the early afternoon. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were -- you told us that you were with your driver on that occasion. Is that correct? Your driver drove you there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the driver was by the vehicle. And only the driver witnessed that scene, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, do you remember if there were any checkpoints in the immediate vicinity of the monastery on the 11th or 12th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether there were any checkpoints. I've said that after the 8th of June 1993, the road to Travnik was open. I arrived from the direction of Zenica on that day. I remember that well. But I can't remember there being any checkpoints on the road. I trusted my driver. I was sure he'd be a good driver. The drivers would change, but I had confidence in my driver. But as to whether there were any checkpoints, I really can't remember. We were never stopped, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if there were any checkpoints run by units of the 3rd Corps in the immediate vicinity of the Guca Gora monastery on the 11th or 12th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was passing through, I don't remember having seen any ABiH checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see or do you remember seeing in the immediate vicinity of the Guca Gora monastery on the 11th or 12th of June 1993 a heavy machine-gun in a sandbagged emplacement?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From where I entered the Guca Gora monastery, I couldn't see a machine-gun nest, not from the direction that I entered the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 11th or 12th of June 1993 when you were at the Guca Gora monastery or the courtyard thereof, did you see any soldiers of any subordinate unit of the 3rd Corps, including any type of military police in the immediate vicinity of that monastery?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the courtyard I entered -- well, I didn't enter the entire courtyard. It was at the beginning of the courtyard that I met this group of foreigners. And there were no ABiH members with them. As to whether there were any such troops on the other side in the immediate vicinity, I don't know. But there were no ABiH members in the area that I entered, apart from my driver who was very near me, but he wasn't actually standing right next to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As your driver approached the monastery and parked the vehicle, did you see any soldiers of any unit of the 3rd Corps in the immediate vicinity of the monastery on the 11th or 12th of June 1993 when you were there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before you enter the courtyard from the eastern side, there is a large bend. And I entered the courtyard -- I can't remember now whether the driver was with me, but he was not in the courtyard with the car. The car was left on the other side of the wall of the convent. And I didn't see any troops in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see any vehicles parked in the immediate vicinity of the monastery in Guca Gora on the 11th or 12th of June 1993? Were there other vehicles parked there when your vehicle approached and your driver parked the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entry -- at the entrance that I used, there were no vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, how long did you remain in the courtyard at the Guca Gora monastery on the 11th or 12th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can remember well, for some four or five hours I was trying to persuade these foreigners to leave the church alone. Not to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us last week that there was a person that you encountered there who spoke Bosnian, and you weren't sure if he was from Bosnia or perhaps somewhere in the former Yugoslavia, but he spoke your language. Is that a fair summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have testified that that person had a beard. He was fair of face. He spoke like a man who lacked the professional terminology, but based on what he was saying I judged that he was a Bosnian, not a foreigner. And since he interpreted whatever the foreigners and I said, I came to the conclusion it was their interpreter who was equally able to communicate with them and with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, other than when you saw this person would spoke Bosnian on the 11th or 12th of June 1993 in the Guca Gora courtyard, or the monastery courtyard, did you ever see that person before that day or did you ever see that person after that day, this person who interpreted for you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw that person either before or after. That was the only time that I saw him at the entrance -- or rather, already in the courtyard of the church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you used this person as an interpreter for the entire four to five hours that you were present on the 11th or 12th of June 1993 in the Guca Gora monastery courtyard?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the only one who interpreted. There was no one else who interpreted. Whether there was anyone else present there who understood Bosnian, I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get that person, the interpreter's, name?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one from that group told me his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I believe you've answered this at least in part, but let me ask you directly: Other than this man who interpreted for you, were there other persons in this group of 10 to 15 people who appeared to you to be Bosnians rather than foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I inferred that, apart from the interpreter, there were no other Bosnians in that group, that all the others were foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, sir, during this four-to-five-hour period on the 11th or 12th of June 1993, did you get to know the names of any one of this group of 10 to 15 persons?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn a single name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 11th or 12th of June 1993, sir, did you or your driver have a Motorola or any other type of radio?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not carry any communication device with me. Maybe the driver did. I don't know what there was in, around the vehicle. It was not my job to know. But maybe the vehicle was equipped for keeping in touch with the superior command. But the vehicle we had did not have any in-built radio so that I should be able to communicate with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, certainly, sir, by this period in June 1993 when you first saw these foreigners, you considered them to be a significant problem for the 3rd Corps, and you've told us that it was -- you considered it to be a law enforcement or a civilian law enforcement problem. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent they were a problem to civilian authorities. The civilian authorities did not share their thoughts with me as to how much of a problem they were to them. I knew that they were a problem to the 3rd Corps, and it was practically the first time that I saw that group of 10 to 15 foreigners. I have already spoken about this. I don't know to what extent they were a problem to civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying, sir, that you don't know if the civilian police would have been the proper authority to deal with these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the security service of the 3rd Corps applied operative methods to find out who those foreigners were. They did that even earlier. Whether the security service had been in touch with civilian authorities, I don't know. Nobody gave me that information. As for operative methods, I'm not an expert. I don't know that the security service of the 3rd Corps talked to the civilian police, but I cannot rule out that they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you report the presence of these people to anyone other than your commander in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only informed the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't recall any efforts taken to contact the civilian security services or the civilian police to get them to go to the monastery in Guca Gora to arrest these people or to take any steps against these people?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally make any such efforts to contact the civilian law enforcement or civilian security services?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian authorities and the civilian police are not the same thing as the security organs of the 3rd Corps. The security organ of the 3rd Corps is a completely different organisation. I also said the civilian police cooperated -- or rather, the police of the 3rd Corps cooperated with the civilian police, but I have no information that they talked on the day of the events in Guca Gora. I spoke to the commander about this, and I know that the 3rd Corps commander had taken steps and that military police had been sent there to secure, to guard the convent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, sir, is a relatively straightforward one: Did you personally contact the civilian police or civilian security services to inform them that there were 10 to 15 foreigners in the courtyard of the Guca Gora monastery shortly after you visited that location on the 11th or 12th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not get in touch with the civilian police or any other civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your indulgence, I have one or two more questions relating to this day, and if we get short answers we should finish here within a minute for today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 11th or 12th of June 1993, did you go inside the monastery at Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On that day, I did not go in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us with respect to the courtyard and the exterior of the monastery building, did you see any visible damage to the monastery? To the exterior of the building or to anything in the courtyard, including any statues or any other items in the courtyard of the monastery or the walls of the courtyard of the monastery, did you see any kind of damage on the 11th or 12th of June 1993 while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I went into the courtyard. I didn't go around the courtyard. From the place where I was standing, I was not able to see any damage on or around the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President, I note the time. We will move on to a different topic tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 7.00 p.m. It's time to terminate this hearing. General, you will come for the hearing tomorrow, tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
